channel.title: Sell to the Past
channel.description: I'm a merchant with a time machine. Each episode I take one thing we buy without thinking and try to sell it to people in the past. How many days of work would they pay? And what does it cost us today? 8 minutes, real numbers with sources.
channel.itunes:author: Sell to the Past

item.title: I tried to sell chocolate to a soldier who gets it free. He paid three rations for one bar
item.description:
I took a bar of chocolate, about three dollars and thirteen cents, into a time machine. I tried to sell it to a porter in Tenochtitlan in 1520, who carried cacao beans as money and was forbidden to drink them; to a day labourer in Williamsburg in 1770, where a hundred grams cost two hours of work; and to an American private in 1942, who got chocolate for free, but chocolate designed not to melt and to taste only a little better than a boiled potato. Who paid the most, and why, says something about what we buy in chocolate.
Chapters: 0:00 The bar and the rules 0:35 Tenochtitlan, 1520: Itzcoatl 3:00 Williamsburg, 1770: Josiah 5:30 An army camp, 1942: Frank 7:30 Back to today
Sources: - Cacao as currency (Mexicolore, Tlaxcala price list 1545): https://www.mexicolore.co.uk/ - Chocolate in colonial Williamsburg (Colonial Williamsburg Foundation): see research/research.md - The Ration D bar (Hershey Community Archives): https://hersheyarchives.org/ - US federal minimum wage: https://www.usa.gov/minimum-wage - All sources are listed in research/research.md of the episode. Backgrounds are AI-generated illustrations made locally; the characters are drawn.

item.title: I tried to sell reading glasses to a monk in 1270. He offered a year of work
item.description:
I took a pair of reading glasses, nine dollars and eighty-nine cents, into a time machine. I tried to sell them to a mercer in the Florence market in 1415, where a pair cost a labourer 37 minutes of work; to a farmer's wife in Iowa in 1897 who ordered from the Sears catalogue for half a day of work; and to a monk and scribe in Tuscany in 1270, when spectacles did not yet exist anywhere in the world, and he offered a year of copying. Who paid the most, and why, says something about what glasses are really worth.
Chapters: 0:00 The glasses and the rules 0:35 Florence, 1415: Bartolomeo 3:00 Iowa, 1897: Ethel 5:30 Tuscany, 1270: Benedetto 7:30 Back to today
Sources: - Vincent Ilardi, Renaissance Vision from Spectacles to Telescopes: see research/research.md - The College of Optometrists museum (early spectacles): https://www.college-optometrists.org/ - Sears catalogue 1897 (spectacles): see research/research.md - Giordano da Pisa's sermon, 1306: see research/research.md - US federal minimum wage: https://www.usa.gov/minimum-wage - All sources are listed in research/research.md of the episode. item.title: I tried to sell a bag of coffee in a camp in 1863. They paid in tobacco
item.description:
I took a bag of coffee, five dollars and fourteen cents, into a time machine. I tried to sell it to a labourer in a London coffeehouse in 1700, where a dish cost a penny and came with a warm room; to a farmer in Prussia in 1777, when King Frederick banned coffee for the people and sent sniffers into the streets; and to a Confederate private in Virginia in 1863, when coffee in the South rose to 196 dollars a pound and soldiers traded tobacco for it between the lines. Who paid the most, and why, says something about what coffee is really worth.
Chapters: 0:00 The bag and the rules 0:35 London, 1700: Ned 3:00 Prussia, 1777: Johann 5:30 Virginia, 1863: Elijah 7:30 Back to today
Sources: - London wages c. 1700 (Judy Stephenson): see research/research.md - Ukers, All About Coffee (Frederick the Great's 1777 manifesto): see research/research.md - Coffee and the Civil War soldier (American Battlefield Trust): https://www.battlefields.org/learn/articles/coffee-and-civil-war-soldier - US coffee price (BLS via FRED): https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/APU0000717311 - US federal minimum wage: https://www.usa.gov/minimum-wage - All sources are listed in research/research.md of the episode. item.title: I tried to sell a paperback in 1835 to a boy who wasn't allowed to read. He paid in bread
item.description:
I took a paperback, nine dollars and ninety-nine cents, into a time machine. I tried to sell it to a mason in Cambridge in 1400, where one manuscript cost more than a hundred days of work; to a clerk in Mainz in 1455, when Gutenberg sold the first printed Bible for three years of wages; and to Frederick, a twelve-year-old boy held in slavery in Baltimore in 1835, when teaching a slave to read was unlawful, and he paid for letters in bread. Who paid the most, and why, says something about what a book is really worth.
Chapters: 0:00 The book and the rules 0:35 Cambridge, 1400: Algar 3:00 Mainz, 1455: Heinrich 5:30 Baltimore, 1835: Frederick 7:30 Back to today
Sources: - Medieval prices (Dyer/Hodges list): https://www.goucher.edu/faculty/awatson/medieval-price-list - The Gutenberg Bible (Cambridge University Library): see research/research.md - Virginia's 1831 anti-literacy law: see research/research.md - Frederick Douglass, Narrative of the Life (1845): see research/research.md - US federal minimum wage: https://www.usa.gov/minimum-wage - All sources are listed in research/research.md of the episode. item.title: I tried to sell a box of matches in a trench in 1916. A soldier offered a week's pay
item.description:
I took a box of matches into a time machine. I tried to sell it to a house servant in Stockton in 1827, when John Walker sold the first box of matches for half a day of work; to a match-factory worker in Bow in 1871, when a halfpenny tax sent thousands marching to Parliament; and to a private in a flooded trench on the Western Front in 1916, when a box cost a penny and no money could buy a dry match. Who paid the most, and why, says something about what fire really costs.
Chapters: 0:00 The box and the rules 0:35 Stockton, 1827: Hannah 3:00 Bow, London, 1871: Alice 5:30 The Western Front, 1916: Arthur 7:30 Back to today
Sources: - John Walker's friction lights (Stockton Heritage): https://heritage.stockton.gov.uk/ - The 1871 match tax (matchgirls1888.org): https://www.matchgirls1888.org/ - British Army pay 1914 (The Long, Long Trail): https://www.longlongtrail.co.uk/ - US federal minimum wage: https://www.usa.gov/minimum-wage - All sources are listed in research/research.md of the episode. item.title: I tried to sell painkillers in 1915. The pharmacist offered everything, and not for the pain
item.description:
I took a box of painkillers, about three dollars and ninety-one cents, into a time machine. I tried to sell it to a mill worker in Manchester in 1845, whose only remedy for a baby's fever was opium; to a druggist in New York in 1932, who sold aspirin in bottles of five thousand; and to a pharmacist in Melbourne in 1915, when the war cut off German aspirin and he was trying to make it himself in kerosene tins. Who offered the most, and why, says something about what we really buy in a pill.

item.title: I tried to sell a T-shirt to a weaver in 1863. He clothed the world and couldn't buy one
item.description:
I took a T-shirt, three dollars and forty-one cents, into a time machine. I tried to sell it to a farm labourer in Rome in 301, when the emperor set a maximum price for a tunic and death for anyone who sold above it; to a spinner in Lancashire in 1745 who earned four pence a day and offered a month of spinning; and to a weaver in Preston in 1863, when the American Civil War stopped the cotton, the mills closed, and families sold their clothes as rags. Who paid the most, and why, says something about the people who make our things.

item.title: I tried to sell a kilo of sugar in 1942. It cost 40 minutes of work, and nobody could buy it
item.description:
I took a kilo of sugar, two dollars and twenty-six cents, into a time machine. I tried to sell it to an apothecary in London in 1319 who sold sugar by the ounce as medicine, to a cane cutter in Jamaica in 1792 who was never paid, and to a mother with a ration book in London in 1942, when sugar was the cheapest in history and nobody could buy more than eight ounces a week. Who paid the most, and why, says something about who is allowed to buy.
Chapters: 0:00 The bag and the rules 0:35 London, 1319: John 3:00 Jamaica, 1792: Kwamina 5:30 London, 1942: Margaret 7:30 Back to today

item.title: I tried to sell a bag of ice in 1595. It cost a month of work, and melted by evening
item.description:
I took a bag of ice, about a dollar twenty, into a time machine. I tried to sell it to a labourer building Lahore fort in 1595, where it cost a month of work; to an Irish ice cutter on the ponds of Massachusetts in 1840, where it cost twenty minutes and he didn't need me; and to a mother in a one-room tenement flat in New York in 1900, when the ice company doubled the price only for small buyers and the mayor held its shares. Who paid the most, and why, says something about who controls a price.

item.title: I tried to sell a lantern in a coal mine in 1842. An 8-year-old paid the most for it
item.description:
I took an LED lantern with its batteries into a time machine. I tried to sell it to a hired hand in Babylon 3,800 years ago, where an hour of light at lantern level cost 34 hours of work; to a stocking knitter in England in 1823, who gave two hours of every working day for taxed candles; and to Tommy, an eight-year-old trapper in a coal mine in 1842, who sat twelve hours in the dark because a candle cost 15% of his wage, and a flame could blow up the mine. Who paid the most, and why, says something about who needs light most.
Chapters: 0:00 The lantern and the rules 0:35 Babylon, 1750 BC: Ili-idinnam 3:00 England, 1823: Martha 5:30 A coal mine, 1842: Tommy 7:30 Back to today
Sources: - Laws of Eshnunna (wages and oil prices): see research/research.md - William Nordhaus, "Do Real-Output and Real-Wage Measures Capture Reality? item.title: I tried to sell a bag of salt in 1784. A kilo cost a day of work, and two minutes across the river
item.description:
I took a bag of salt, two dollars and forty-nine cents, into a time machine. I tried to sell it to a builder in Rome in 301, to a day labourer in Berry in 1784 who lived across the river from salt ten times cheaper, and to a farm labourer in India in April 1930, on the road to Dandi. Who paid the most, and why, says something about who really controls a price.

item.title: I tried to sell a litre of water to a man who sells water in 1854. Then I said one word
item.description:
I took a one-litre bottle of tap water, worth a fifth of a cent in the US, into a time machine. I tried to sell it to a water carrier in cholera-era London, to a water carrier in Paris before the Revolution, and to a sailor in the middle of the ocean in 1812. Who paid the most, and why, says something about what water really costs.
Chapters: 0:00 The bottle and the rules 0:35 London, 1854: William 3:00 Paris, 1785: Jacques 5:30 The ocean, 1812: Tom 7:30 Back to today

Images: Wikimedia Commons, public domain / CC (credit on screen).

item.title: I tried to sell a supermarket loaf of bread to people in 1795. Here's what they paid
item.description: A standard sliced loaf costs about $2.30 in the US, or 19 minutes of work at the federal minimum wage. In this first episode I take it into a time machine and try to sell it three times: to a farm labourer in England in the hungry summer of 1795, where a loaf cost five hours in the field; to a builder in Rome in 301 AD, where the wheat in a loaf cost two hours but white bread was status; and to a clerk in Paris under siege in 1870, where 300 grams a day were rationed and no money bought more. The best buyer wasn't the richest. All numbers with sources in the description.
